newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Pertamina eyes government help to build refineries.
newsitem.headline: Pertamina eyes government help to build refineries.

text.p: Indonesia's state-owned Pertamina, suffering from limited funds and poor refining profits, needs financial support from the central government to build new oil refineries, a Pertamina official said on Tuesday.
"I think it is very difficult for us to build new grassroot refineries," Nyoman Sudibia, Pertamina's vice president for planning and budgeting, told Reuters in an interview.
"We need to have enough investments for it, but this is also one of the constraints as each refinery costs about $2 billion. But if the government would like to participate we will be very happy."
Pertamina has told the government that along with rising oil product demand, especially diesel, Pertamina needs to import 65 million barrels a year or about five million barrels a month, he said.
If no new refineries were built, Indonesia's oil product imports would grow at a rate of five percent a year, said Sudibia who was in Singapore to speak at a fuel and lubricants conference.
Pertamina would import 10 million kilolitres of oil products in fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) up from seven million kilolitres in 1996/97, the company said earlier.
Sudibia said there has not been "any signals from the government whether or not they are willing to participate" in building refineries.
Indonesia, Asia's sole member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), also imports 65 million barrels of crude a year, mainly from the Middle East.
Indonesia's refineries, all of them state-owned, have a total capacity of 989,900 barrels per day (bpd).

Pertamina's president-director Faisal Abda'oe had said earlier this month that Indonesia needed two more oil refineries by 2000 to meet growing demand for fuel oil products and Pertamina was ready to build new refineries if the government gave the green light.
Sudibia said it would also be difficult for the private sector to build new refineries because refining margins have been very low in Indonesia.
For example, Indonesian refineries suffered losses last year and were at break-even so far this year, he said.

Other reasons are that the private sector needs to ensure a stable supply of crude and secure outlets in the domestic market for their refined products before committing themselves to developing the refineries.

Sudibia said several private firms have shown interest to build new refineries with average capacity of 125,000-150,000 bpd each -- three parties in South Sulawesi, four in East Java, one in West Java and and one each in Lombok and Irian Jaya.

But industry sources said the private sector was still waiting for the government to pass deregulation laws allowing them to sell oil products at market prices rather than government-determined prices before starting the projects.

On its plans to venture overseas, Sudibia said Pertamina is having "very intensive discussions with Burma for oil and gas exploration and downstream activities." This is being done through its affiliate companies like Perta Oil.
Preliminary talks are also being held with Cambodia, he said.
